headline: Three prediction-market operators halt Connecticut sports contracts amid state crackdown
dek: State officials say three of nine companies targeted over unlicensed sports wagering have stopped offering prediction-market services in Connecticut, but the scope of at least one departure remains disputed.
body: Connecticut regulators say three of the nine prediction-market operators targeted in the state's September crackdown have stopped offering sports-event contracts to residents, giving the state's campaign against a fast-growing form of online wagering its first reported retreat. The development affects platforms that let users buy and sell contracts tied to sports outcomes, while leaving six other named operators in communication with the Department of Consumer Protection.

The [Connecticut Office of the Governor](https://portal.ct.gov/governor/news/press-releases/2026/09-2026/governor-lamont-announces-new-actions-against-illegal-prediction-markets-offering-sports-wagers) said the Department of Consumer Protection issued nine cease-and-desist orders in September. The agency's list included Polymarket, Coinbase, Crypto.com, Robinhood, ProphetX, Novig, Webull, Gemini and Underdog Predict. The orders directed the platforms to stop advertising, promoting or making unlicensed online gambling available to Connecticut residents. They also required the platforms to let Connecticut customers withdraw funds held on their services.

The new development was reported by Connecticut news outlets after DCP Commissioner Bryan Cafferelli said three operators had heard the state's message and were leaving. [CT Insider reported](https://www.ctinsider.com/politics/article/prediction-market-companies-leave-ct-22460358.php) that officials identified the three as ProphetX, Gemini and Webull. The story said the department remained in contact with Polymarket, Coinbase, Crypto.com, Robinhood, Novig and Underdog. A related [News-Times report](https://www.newstimes.com/politics/article/connecticut-prediction-market-companies-leave-ct-22460358.php) clarified that Webull intended to continue its other services in Connecticut and was responding specifically to the order concerning prediction markets.

That distinction matters because “leaving Connecticut” can describe several different actions: shutting down a company's entire business in the state, removing only sports contracts, or restricting particular products through geolocation. The News-Times report said an analyst disputed the characterization of ProphetX's withdrawal, while Webull said it was still operating other services. The public statements reviewed for this report therefore support a narrower conclusion: state officials say three operators have stopped or are stopping the targeted sports-market activity, but the exact product-by-product status is not independently established for every company.

Connecticut's position is that sports prediction markets are wagers, not investments insulated from state gaming rules. The governor's September announcement said the state believes the contracts can take bets from people under 21, people on the voluntary self-exclusion list and participants wagering on Connecticut college sports. Officials also said the platforms do not operate under the technical, integrity and consumer-protection standards required of licensed sportsbooks. Those are the state's allegations and regulatory conclusions; the companies have argued that their event contracts are financial products governed by federal law.

The fight has regional and national significance because prediction markets have expanded beyond election-style questions into contracts on game winners, point spreads and player statistics. Connecticut's release said one platform reported nearly $250 million in college-football trading volume on the first day of the 2026 season. The state is trying to preserve a more limited legal market created in 2021, when Connecticut authorized sports wagering through licensed partners connected to DraftKings, FanDuel and Fanatics, while maintaining an age minimum and responsible-gambling rules.

The enforcement campaign also sits alongside a court dispute. Connecticut sued Kalshi in August seeking to block what the attorney general described as unlicensed sports betting. In its [August 26 announcement](https://portal.ct.gov/ag/press-releases/2026-press-releases/connecticut-sues-kalshi-to-stop-illegal-unlicensed-sports-betting), the attorney general's office said a federal judge had denied Kalshi's request for a preliminary injunction and that Kalshi had appealed to the Second Circuit. The Kalshi litigation is separate from the September orders to the nine operators, but it could help determine how far state gambling laws reach when a platform describes its products as federally regulated event contracts.

For Connecticut users, the immediate practical question is access to specific sports markets and the ability to withdraw money, not whether all prediction-market products have disappeared. The department said it is still communicating with six operators, and the state has not announced a final resolution with each of them. Further cease-and-desist actions, company notices, court rulings or public compliance records will be needed to show whether the remaining platforms restrict their sports offerings or continue to challenge Connecticut's interpretation of state law.
